rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ 'Stationary orbit' means the electron is at rest. ✅ The electron moves, but the orbit is stationary *in energy* — it does not radiate.  ·  ❌ Bohr orbits and orbitals are the same. ✅ Orbits are fixed 2D circular paths of definite radius/energy; orbitals are 3D probability regions from the Schrödinger equation.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Bohr radius a₀ = 0.529 Å = 52.9 pm; ground-state speed of the H electron = 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ = c/137.  ·  Ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹; ionisation energy of He⁺ = 54.4 eV.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Radius and energy of the electron in the n = 2 orbit of Li²⁺. **Solution:** r₂ = 0.529 × 2²/3 = 0.705 Å = 70.5 pm; E₂ = −13.6 × 3²/2² = −30.6 eV.  ·  **Problem:** Energy to excite H from n = 1 to n = 3? **Solution:** ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/9) = 12.09 eV; λ = 1240/12.09 ≈ 102.6 nm (Lyman series).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: postulates of bohr's atomic model, its application (within Atomic Structure).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning — why a new model was needed  ·  Rutherford's nuclear model could not explain (i) why the revolving electron does not fall into the nucleus and (ii) why hydrogen gives discrete spectral lines. In 1913 Niels Bohr combined classical mechanics with Planck's quantum theory for the hydrogen atom and other one-electron species (He⁺, Li²⁺).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Ground-state energy of hydrogen = −13.6 eV, and level spacing decreases as 1/n² increases.  ·  Bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy En = −13.6 eV·Z²/n² (for H, Z=1).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: state + explain the main idea of "Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application" with one example.  ·  compare "Postulates of Bohr's atomic model" with the related idea from a neighbouring unit.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Quote all four postulates; the marks sit on 'stationary orbit', 'mvr = nh/2π' and 'hν = E₂ − E₁'.  ·  Negative total energy signals a bound state — always mention that the zero of energy is taken at infinite separation.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Postulates of Bohr's atomic model  ·  • Its application

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Rydberg/Balmer series: 1/λ = R(H)(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Absorption/emission = ΔE = hν between levels.  ·  Four quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0…n−1), mₗ (orientation, −l…+l), mₛ (spin ±½). Orbitals: s (spherical), p (dumbbell).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: solve / apply for "Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application" and verify the answer is plausible.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Worked: identify given → pick sub-concept → apply standard form → check units / edges.  ·  **Problem:** Energy to excite He⁺ from n = 1 to n = 2. **Solution:** ΔE = 13.6 × 2² × (1 − 1/4) = 13.6 × 4 × 0.75 = 40.8 eV — three times the corresponding H value, because of the Z² factor.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A common examiner point on "Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application" is that a statement is only valid when its condition of applicability is met. Is that TRUE or FALSE? → True  ·  The radius of the 2nd Bohr orbit of Li²⁺ is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Postulates of Bohr's model (state them in order)  ·  • **Stationary orbits:** the electron revolves only in certain permitted circular orbits (stationary states) of definite energy and does **not** radiate while in such an orbit.  ·  • **Quantisation of angular momentum:** only orbits with mvr = nh/2π are allowed, n = 1, 2, 3, … (n = principal quantum number).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1},\qquad \bar{\nu}=RZ^{2}\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)$$  ·  En(H) = −13.6 Z²/n² eV  ·  hν = ΔE

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: λ = h/(mv) (de Broglie)  ·  $$E_{n}=-13.6\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV},\qquad IE_{n}=13.6\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}$$  ·  $$\lambda(\text{nm})=\frac{1240}{\Delta E(\text{eV})}$$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi},\qquad \frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{kZe^{2}}{r^{2}},\qquad h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1}$$  ·  $$h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1}=13.6\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)\ \text{eV}$$  ·  $$\text{emission: }n_{2}\rightarrow n_{1}\ (\downarrow);\qquad \text{absorption: }n_{1}\rightarrow n_{2}\ (\uparrow)$$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$E_{n}=-13.6\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV};\qquad KE=-E_{n};\qquad PE=2E_{n}$$  ·  $$\text{IE from level }n=|E_{n}|=13.6\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}$$  ·  ❌ A bound electron has positive energy. ✅ Its energy is negative (zero at infinite separation).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Bohr's model works for all atoms. ✅ Only for one-electron species: H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺.  ·  ❌ The electron radiates while revolving in an allowed orbit. ✅ Radiation occurs only during a jump.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy en = −13.6 ev·z²/n² (for h, z=1)..
